meta.title: Bacterial Genetics & Bacteriophage Biology
meta.summary: Bacteria are haploid and reproduce asexually by binary fission, but they can still acquire new genetic material from other cells or from their environment...

blocks.x: Bacteria are haploid and reproduce asexually by binary fission, but they can still acquire new genetic material from other cells or from their environment through three classical mechanisms of horizontal (lateral) gene transfer: transformation, conjugation, and transduction. All three mechanisms depend on host Rec proteins (notably RecA) to carry out the actual recombination that integrates incoming DNA into the recipient's chromosome, so recombination-deficient (rec⁻) strains cannot stably acquire new genes even when DNA enters the cell.
Transformation

Transformation is the direct uptake of naked, "free" DNA from the surrounding environment by a competent bacterial cell. The DNA usually comes from lysed donor cells. Once inside, single strands can recombine with the homologous region of the recipient chromosome. Transformation is historically important: Frederick Griffith (1928) first demonstrated it using Diplococcus pneumoniae (now classified as Streptococcus pneumoniae), showing that heat-killed virulent (S, smooth) bacteria could transfer a "transforming principle" to live avirulent (R, rough) bacteria, converting them to virulent. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944) later showed biochemically that this transforming principle was DNA, not protein — the first direct evidence that DNA is the genetic material. Only some bacterial species are naturally competent (e.g. Streptococcus, Bacillus, Haemophilus, Neisseria); others are made "artificially competent" in the lab using calcium chloride treatment (heat shock) or electroporation, which is the basis of transforming E. coli with plasmids in genetic engineering.
Conjugation

Conjugation is direct, cell-to-cell transfer of DNA through physical contact, mediated by the F (fertility) plasmid. A cell carrying the F plasmid (F+) assembles a hair-like appendage called the sex pilus, which attaches to an F- recipient cell and draws the two cells together (or, in some models, forms a conduit) so that DNA can pass through. During conjugation, the F plasmid is nicked at its origin of transfer (oriT) and a single strand is transferred to the recipient in a rolling-circle fashion; both donor and recipient then synthesize the complementary strand, so an F+ x F- mating typically converts the recipient to F+ as well, usually without transferring chromosomal genes.

The F plasmid is a circular, double-stranded, autonomously replicating DNA element that exists as one (or a small number of) copies free in the cytoplasm in F<sup>+</sup> cells. Key facts examiners like to test: the F factor is composed of circular DNA; there is generally about one copy per cell; and its transfer functions are independent of the transmission of chromosomal genes (i.e., F transfer does not require chromosomal gene transfer to occur) — this is different from the situation in Hfr strains.

Occasionally the F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome by homologous recombination between insertion sequences shared by the plasmid and the chromosome. A cell with an integrated F plasmid is called an Hfr (high frequency of recombination) strain, because conjugation from an Hfr donor now drags along a strand of chromosomal DNA behind the mobilized F DNA, transferring chromosomal genes into the recipient at high frequency (though the F factor itself, at the trailing end, is transferred last and is usually lost before the process, which takes about 100 minutes for the whole E. coli chromosome, completes — so the recipient is rarely converted to F+ in an Hfr cross). The order and timing with which markers appear in the recipient can be used to map the bacterial chromosome ("interrupted mating" experiments). An F plasmid that excises imprecisely from an Hfr chromosome can pick up adjacent bacterial genes, becoming an F' (F-prime) plasmid that carries chromosomal DNA and can transfer those genes at high efficiency to new recipients — a mechanism related to specialized transduction in phages.
Transduction

Transduction is the transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another using a bacteriophage as the vehicle — it is virus-mediated DNA transfer, and it is often described as being "akin to lysogeny" because it typically arises from errors during the lysogenic/lytic cycle of a temperate phage.

items: Generalized transduction: occurs when, during the lytic cycle, the phage packaging machinery mistakenly packages a fragment of host chromosomal DNA (of about phage-genome size) into a phage capsid instead of phage DNA. Because packaging errors can occur anywhere along the chromosome, essentially any bacterial gene can be transferred this way. When such a particle infects a new host, it injects bacterial DNA rather than phage DNA, which can then recombine into the new host's chromosome. Phage P1 and P22 are classic generalized transducing phages.

Specialized (restricted) transduction: occurs with temperate phages (like lambda) that integrate at a specific chromosomal site. If the prophage excises imprecisely during induction, it can carry adjacent host genes packaged together with phage DNA (analogous to F' plasmid formation). Because lambda always integrates at the same attB site (between the gal and bio operons on the E. coli chromosome), specialized transduction by lambda can only transfer genes near that site (e.g. gal or bio), unlike the essentially random gene transfer of generalized transduction.

blocks.x: Plasmids are small, typically circular, double-stranded, extrachromosomal DNA molecules capable of autonomous replication, found across all three domains of life — Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya all contain organisms with plasmids. In bacteria they may carry genes for antibiotic resistance (R-plasmids), virulence factors, metabolic pathways for unusual substrates (e.g. the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens, used to genetically engineer plants), or conjugative transfer functions (like F).

Plasmids are the workhorse cloning vectors of genetic engineering, and are the most commonly used vector overall. pBR322 is the best-known, "classic" cloning plasmid, engineered with an origin of replication, an ampicillin-resistance gene and a tetracycline-resistance gene (allowing selection of transformants and screening of inserts by insertional inactivation). Historically, pSC101 was the plasmid vector used in the very first genetic-engineering (recombinant DNA) experiment in 1973 by Cohen, Boyer, Chang, and Helling. When a foreign ("passenger") DNA segment is ligated into a plasmid, the resulting hybrid plasmid carrying the insert is called recombinant DNA, while the plasmid backbone itself is referred to as the vector DNA. Besides plasmids, other vectors used in genetic engineering include bacteriophage vectors (the largest number of phage cloning vectors are derived from lambda phage), cosmids (plasmid–phage hybrids), and the large-insert vectors YAC (yeast artificial chromosome) and BAC (bacterial artificial chromosome). Note that in Gram-positive bacteria, only plasmids (not phage-based vectors) are generally used as cloning vectors, since phage biology in Gram-positives differs substantially from the well-worked-out Gram-negative (E. coli) phage systems.

Bacteriophages ("phages") are viruses that infect bacteria — by definition they are bacterial viruses. The term "bacteriophage" (meaning "bacteria eater") was coined by Félix d'Hérelle, who independently characterized them in 1917. However, phages were first discovered slightly earlier, in 1915, by the English bacteriologist Frederick W. Twort, who observed the same lytic phenomenon in staphylococci. (d'Hérelle is credited with naming them and firmly establishing them as viruses; Twort gets priority of discovery — quizzes often test both names separately.)

A typical (tailed) phage virion has a protein capsid/head that packages the genetic material, and in many phages a tail ending in tail fibers. Tail fibers are specifically responsible for attachment (adsorption) of the phage to specific receptor molecules on the bacterial cell surface — these host receptors can be lipopolysaccharide (LPS), teichoic acid, outer-membrane proteins, or even flagella/pili, depending on the phage; i.e., all of these categories serve as phage receptors in different systems. After attachment, the tail (in contractile-tailed phages) contracts to drive a tube through the cell envelope and inject the genome, leaving the empty capsid outside ("penetration").

Phage genetic material can be any of the four possible nucleic-acid types: double-stranded DNA (the great majority of tailed phages, e.g. lambda, T4, T7), single-stranded DNA (e.g. ΦX174, M13), double-stranded RNA (e.g. Φ6), or single-stranded RNA (e.g. MS2, R17, f2, Qβ — the RNA coliphages of E. coli). This diversity is often tested as "the genetic material of bacteriophage is: All (i.e., dsDNA, ssDNA, or ssRNA depending on the phage)."

Bacteriophages generally lack peptidoglycan — peptidoglycan is a bacterial cell-wall component, not a phage structure, so it is the odd one out among phage-related terms such as lysogenic cycle, endolysin, and prophage. An unusual chemical feature of some phage genomes is the presence of modified bases: 5-hydroxymethylcytosine replaces ordinary cytosine as a normal DNA constituent in T-even phages such as T2 (and T4, T6), which protects the phage DNA from the host's restriction enzymes.
The Lytic and Lysogenic Cycles

Phages fall into two broad categories by lifestyle. Virulent (lytic) phages can only replicate via the lytic cycle and always kill the host. Temperate phages (such as lambda, P1, P22, and Mu) can follow either pathway: the lytic cycle or the lysogenic cycle — so tailed temperate phages exhibit both lytic and lysogenic cycles depending on conditions. Mu phage is notable as a large transposable phage — it replicates by transposing itself repeatedly into the host chromosome.

c: Replicates independently in the cytoplasm; directs synthesis of new virions
Integrates into the host chromosome (or persists as a plasmid) as a prophage
Host is destroyed (lysed) to release progeny phage
Host survives and divides normally, passing the prophage to daughter cells
Nearly all phage genes expressed in a temporal cascade (early → middle → late)
Almost all phage genes repressed; typically only the repressor gene (cI in lambda) is expressed
Lysogen is immune to superinfection by the same phage (repressor blocks it)
Induction (e.g. DNA damage/SOS response) can activate lytic genes and cause the prophage to excise and enter the lytic cycle
Cell lysis via endolysin (breaks down peptidoglycan) often paired with holin (permeabilizes membrane)
Ends when induction occurs, switching to lytic cycle

blocks.x: Phage release from the host cell occurs by several routes depending on the phage: most tailed phages lyse the cell using endolysin; filamentous phages (e.g. M13) are extruded continuously without killing the cell; and some enveloped phages bud from the membrane — so "bacteriophages are released via cell lysis, budding, or extrusion" are all correct, i.e., all of the above. The specific lytic enzyme that degrades the peptidoglycan cell wall to allow phage escape is called endolysin (distinct from terminase, which is the enzyme complex that recognizes and cuts concatemeric phage DNA and actively packages/translocates it into the preformed capsid — an ATP-driven "molecular motor").

Lysogeny is favored (i.e., temperate phage is more likely to lysogenize rather than lyse) under conditions such as a high multiplicity of infection (many phages infecting one cell simultaneously) and when the host cells are nutritionally starved/poor (stressed) — both of these conditions favor lysogeny (poor host growth conditions make survival of the phage genome, rather than immediate lytic replication, the safer strategy).
Lambda (λ) Phage

Lambda is a temperate phage of E. coli and the best-studied genetic switch in molecular biology, and the source of the largest number of bacteriophage cloning vectors used in genetic engineering. Its dsDNA genome is linear inside the virion but has complementary single-stranded "sticky ends" (cos sites); upon infection, the injected linear DNA circularizes by base-pairing of these cohesive ends, and this circular form is a substrate for both replication and site-specific integration into the host chromosome.

The central genetic switch that decides lysis versus lysogeny is controlled by a small regulatory region containing two divergent promoters, PRM (for repressor maintenance) and PR (rightward promoter, driving cro), which overlap three operator sites arranged as OR1 – OR2 – OR3. The overall gene order along the chromosome in this region is often quoted as cI gene – OR3 – OR2 – OR1 – cro gene, with cI transcribed leftward from OR3 and cro transcribed rightward from OR1.

items: cI (repressor): the master lysogeny-maintenance protein. cI dimers bind cooperatively to the operators, with highest affinity for OR1 and OR2. Bound at OR1/OR2, cI blocks RNA polymerase from using PR (so cro and downstream lytic genes are off) while simultaneously activating its own transcription from PRM — a classic autoregulatory positive-and-negative feedback loop that maintains stable lysogeny. cI is the only phage protein expressed at significant levels in a stable lysogen.

cro: the "control of repressor and other things" protein, which acts in the opposite sense — cro binds the same operators but with reversed affinity (highest for OR3), which turns off PRM (shutting down more cI synthesis) and eventually allows PR to be used, driving the lytic cascade. Cro is a repressor only — it has no activating (positive) function, unlike cI, which both represses PR and activates PRM. When neither cro nor cI (repressor) is bound at OR, RNA polymerase can transcribe freely from PR.

N: an antitermination protein and RNA-binding factor. It binds RNA polymerase (via interaction with nascent RNA nut sites) and allows the polymerase to read through transcription terminators, extending transcripts into the "delayed early" genes. Antitermination of this type is a regulatory strategy essentially unique to lambda (and related phages) among the classic model phages (contrasted with T7, ΦX174, T4).
Q: a second antiterminator, acting later, that allows transcription to proceed into the late (structural/lysis) genes from the PR' promoter.

cII and cIII: cII is a transcriptional activator that turns on the promoters needed to establish lysogeny (including driving cI expression via PRE, the "establishment" promoter, and driving the integrase gene int), but cII protein is very unstable — it is rapidly degraded by host proteases (notably FtsH/HflB). cIII protects cII from this proteolytic degradation, stabilizing it long enough to establish lysogeny. Because the decision to lysogenize versus lyse hinges on whether enough active cII accumulates, cro and cII are considered the two genes most critical in determining the developmental fate (lysis vs. lysogeny) of the phage.

int / xis: Int (integrase) catalyzes site-specific recombination between the phage attP site and the bacterial attB site to integrate the prophage; Xis (excisionase) is required together with Int to catalyze the reverse reaction, excision of the prophage during induction.

blocks.x: Because temperate phage genetics can be complex, characterizing lambda mutants classically required complementation tests (to determine how many distinct genes/cistrons are affected), mapping (to order the mutations along the genome), and dominance tests (to characterize the mutant allele's behavior relative to wild type) — cloning the genes themselves is a modern convenience, not a step that was essential to classical mutant characterization.
T4 and T7 Phage

T4 is a large, virulent, contractile-tailed dsDNA phage of E. coli with a complex genome (~300 kb, ~300 genes) and an elaborate, highly cooperative assembly pathway (head, tail, and tail-fiber sub-assemblies join independently before combining) — much of what is known about self-assembly and gene-protein colinearity came from classic T4 genetics by Alfred Hershey and Seymour Benzer (both Nobel-relevant/renowned researchers on T4); Sydney Brenner, Francis Crick, and others also used T4 rII mutants to establish the triplet nature of the genetic code, while James Watson's major fame lies elsewhere (DNA structure), which is why "Watson" is sometimes flagged as the odd one out among Nobel-caliber names associated with T4 research.

T7 phage, by contrast, has a much smaller, simpler, and highly efficient genome (~40 kb) that is a favorite model for synthetic biology because of its economical genetic organization and strict temporal transcription program driven by its own phage-encoded RNA polymerase. A hallmark feature of T7 is its gene 5 product, gp5, which — together with the host protein thioredoxin as a processivity factor — forms the highly processive T7 DNA polymerase. (This gp5/thioredoxin complex was engineered into the commercial enzyme "Sequenase," widely used for DNA sequencing.) T7-based expression systems are a cornerstone of modern synthetic biology and recombinant protein production (e.g. many "pET" vectors rely on T7 RNA polymerase), so T7 phage is correctly associated with gp5 DNA polymerase, synthetic biology applications, and (unrelated, but a name overlap tested in some quizzes) is not to be confused with the pathogenic E. coli strain O157:H7.
ΦX174 (Phi X 174)

ΦX174 is a small, icosahedral bacteriophage of E. coli with a circular single-stranded DNA genome (~5,400 nucleotides). It holds a special place in the history of genetics and biotechnology: it was the first DNA genome to be fully sequenced (Fred Sanger's group, 1977), and it was here that overlapping genes were first discovered — some of its genes are encoded within the same stretch of DNA as other genes but read in a different reading frame, so a single DNA sequence encodes more than one protein. This packs more coding capacity into its very small genome. ΦX174 is not the most mutable virus in general knowledge (that distinction, among commonly quizzed viruses, goes to HIV, a retrovirus with an error-prone reverse transcriptase and no proofreading).
Other Notable Phages

The RNA coliphages of E. coli — MS2, R17, f2, and Qβ — are small icosahedral phages with positive-sense single-stranded RNA genomes; MS2 was historically important as the first genome (of any organism) to be completely sequenced (1976, at the RNA level). Structurally and biochemically, small icosahedral bacteriophages such as MS2, ΦX174, and PRD1 are often noted to resemble simple pathogenic human enteric viruses (e.g. picornaviruses) in overall architecture, which makes them convenient models for studying capsid assembly and enteric virus behavior/environmental persistence.

items: Virion — a complete, infectious extracellular phage particle.
Prophage — the dormant phage genome integrated into (or otherwise stably maintained within) a lysogenic host.
Induction — the process by which a prophage is triggered to excise and re-enter the lytic cycle (commonly induced by DNA damage / the SOS response, e.g. from UV light).
Adsorption — the initial, specific attachment of a phage to its host-cell surface receptor.
Terminase — the enzyme complex that packages replicated phage DNA into preformed capsids.
Endolysin — the enzyme that degrades host peptidoglycan to allow cell lysis and phage release.
Recombinant/passenger/vector DNA — respectively, the hybrid molecule, the inserted foreign fragment, and the carrier plasmid/phage backbone used in cloning.
